title: Betta Buoyancy Problems: Swim Bladder Triage | BettaFish.website
description: Assess floating, sinking and rolling in a betta without assuming constipation or prescribing one fasting treatment for every cause.
h1: Betta Buoyancy Problems: Swim Bladder Triage
intro: Floating, sinking, rolling or struggling to hold position describes a buoyancy problem, not one disease. Digestive distension, infection, injury, developmental change, masses, fluid imbalance and gas-bladder damage can produce similar signs. Start with water tests and a whole-fish assessment, then choose treatment by the suspected cause.

sections.heading: Loss of function can be urgent

text.text: Seek prompt aquatic-veterinary help when a betta cannot reach air or food, rolls continuously, breathes rapidly, has marked swelling or pineconing, shows bleeding or trauma, or declines quickly. Gas-bladder surgery and imaging are veterinary procedures, not home interventions.

sections.heading: How should a buoyancy problem be assessed?

steps.title: Test the environment
steps.text: Measure temperature, ammonia, nitrite, nitrate and pH; verify heater, filter and aeration operation.

steps.title: Record the exact movement
steps.text: Video whether the fish floats, sinks, lists, rolls, struggles after effort or rests normally between episodes.

steps.title: Review food and output
steps.text: Record the last several meals, portion changes, feces and abdominal shape without assuming constipation.

steps.title: Reduce physical demands
steps.text: Provide calm water, unobstructed surface access and safe resting points while maintaining heat and water quality.

steps.title: Escalate persistent or severe signs
steps.text: Share videos, measurements and history with an aquatic veterinarian; ask whether imaging, microscopy or other diagnostics are indicated.

sections.heading: Should every floating betta be fasted?

paragraphs.text: No. A short feeding pause may be part of a plan when recent overfeeding and temporary abdominal distension are plausible, but universal multi-day fasting can delay care for infection, injury, fluid accumulation or another internal problem.

Do not feed peas as a default remedy. Bettas are insectivorous-carnivorous fish, and a pea does not diagnose or correct every cause of buoyancy loss. A clinician may recommend an appropriate food, portion or fasting interval after reviewing the case.

sections.heading: How can the aquarium be made safer during recovery?

paragraphs.text: Keep the fish in a heated, covered and biologically managed system with gentle flow. Add broad smooth resting surfaces at several heights and remove sharp objects or narrow gaps.

A modestly reduced water depth may help a fish reach the surface, but a tiny unfiltered container creates new temperature and waste risks. Change depth only while preserving stable heat, oxygenation, filtration and sufficient horizontal movement.

items.question: Is swim bladder disease one disease?
items.answer: No. The phrase is commonly used for a visible buoyancy problem that can have digestive, infectious, traumatic, developmental or internal causes.

items.question: Why is my betta floating on its side?
items.answer: Side-floating can follow temporary distension, gas-bladder dysfunction or serious systemic disease. Test the water and assess breathing, swelling, appetite, feces and duration rather than assuming one cause.

items.question: Will daphnia cure a swim bladder problem?
items.answer: Daphnia may be an appropriate food in some feeding plans, but it does not treat infection, trauma, a mass or gas-bladder damage. Do not use one food as a diagnostic test.

items.question: Should I move the fish to shallow water?
items.answer: Shallower water can reduce effort for selected fish, but only if temperature, oxygenation, filtration and water quality remain stable. Use a clinician's plan for a severely impaired fish.

items.question: Can a veterinarian treat a damaged swim bladder?
items.answer: Depending on the cause, a veterinarian may use examination, imaging, medical care or, in selected larger fish, gas-bladder procedures. MSD describes gas-bladder repair as a surgical veterinary option.
